extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students learning discrete mathematics and proof techniques
extracted.subtask_description: Writing and checking solutions to discrete-mathematics exercises (induction proofs, divisibility, relations, functions, combinatorics, pigeonhole applications) typical of an introductory undergraduate textbook. Emphasises correct proof structure and standard algebraic/elementwise manipulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by mathematical induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove a statement for all integers n ≥ base by (1) verifying the base case, (2) assuming the statement for n = k (inductive hypothesis), and (3) showing the statement holds for n = k + 1, concluding 'Thus the result follows by mathematical induction.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: sums of powers and products (Problems 7, 9, 11, 13, 15, etc.). Show base case explicitly (often n=0 or n=1), substitute the inductive hypothesis into the expression for k+1, simplify algebraically to obtain the claimed closed form. Conclude by standard induction phrase. Pay attention to correct algebraic manipulation when adding the (k+1)-th term.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strong induction
rubrics_metrics.description: When using strong induction, verify initial base(s) (e.g., n=2), assume the statement true for all values up to k, then prove it for k+1 using the full assumption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: set intersection/union identity (Problem 17). Demonstrate how combining previous cases (≤ k) gives the k+1 case. Make sure basis covers smallest needed values and state the induction hypothesis correctly (for all m ≤ k).

rubrics_metrics.name: Verifying divisibility statements
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove a|P(n) for all n (or for n≥0), show expression equals a times some integer; often by representing P(k) = a·t then manipulating to get P(k+1)=a·(something).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 24 | (5^{2n} − 1) (Problem 9) where assume 5^{2k} − 1 = 24a then compute 5^{2(k+1)} − 1 and factor to exhibit a multiple of 24. Emphasise solving for an integer multiplier and using algebraic identities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving congruences/divisibility by factoring/grouping
rubrics_metrics.description: Rewrite expressions (k+1)^3 + ... etc, group terms to factor out the modulus (e.g., factor 3) and conclude divisibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: show 3 | (n^3 + 5n + 6) by expanding (k+1)^3, collecting (k^3+5k+6) and the remaining terms, then factoring out 3 to produce 3·(integer). State explicitly that the remaining parenthesised quantity is integer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving closed-form sum identities by induction and algebraic simplification
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume closed form holds for k, add the (k+1)-th term and algebraically manipulate to show the closed form for k+1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: sum formulas for 1·3 + 2·4 + ... (Problem 7), harmonic-like telescoping sums 1/(n(n+1)) = 1 - 1/(n+1) (Problem 15). Use algebraic factorisation and common denominators; for telescoping show cancellation pattern explicitly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving inequalities via grouping and bounds (used in induction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish lower/upper bounds for grouped terms and then use induction on n to extend the inequality by showing an increment preserves the bound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: bounding partial harmonic sums by grouping terms and using trivial lower bounds for each group. Clearly state why each grouped term meets the bound and how many groups appear when passing from n to n+1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Pascal's identity and binomial coefficient identities
rubrics_metrics.description: Use identities (n choose r) = (n−1 choose r−1) + (n−1 choose r) (Pascal) and boundary/zero conventions to manipulate binomial sums and prove combinatorial identities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: binomial theorem induction (Problem 23) and sum identity (Problem 31). When regrouping sums, apply Pascal's identity and verify index ranges; note the convention that binomial coefficients are zero when indices are out of range.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving the binomial theorem by induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Base n=1 check, assume (x+y)^n = sum_{i=0}^n (n choose i) x^{n−i} y^i, multiply by (x+y) and use Pascal's identity to obtain the n+1 expansion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show term-by-term expansion, regroup powers of x and y, apply coefficient identities to recombine coefficients into (n+1 choose i). Make boundary terms explicit (x^{n+1} and y^{n+1}).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving Fibonacci identities by induction using the recurrence
rubrics_metrics.description: Verify base cases (n=1, n=2), assume identity for k (or k and k−1 for strong), then use F_{n+2}=F_{n+1}+F_n to manipulate sums to required form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: telescoping sums of Fibonacci numbers (Problems 25, 27, 29). When summing F1+...+Fn use the recurrence to collapse into Fn+2 − 1; check small cases separately if necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parity and even/odd arguments in combinatorial coefficients
rubrics_metrics.description: To show a binomial coefficient is even (or has parity property), use identities to express it as sum of smaller coefficients and apply inductive parity facts or show factors include an even factor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: if n is even and k is odd then (n choose k) is even (Problem 35). Use Pascal-like expansions repeatedly to reduce to previously known even quantities and note when a factor k(k+1) is even.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elementwise set equality proofs using definitions and logical equivalences
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove A = B by manipulating set-definitions (membership, complements, De Morgan, distribution) to show any x ∈ A iff x ∈ B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: showing intersection equals union via complement and De Morgan (Problem 17). Start from one side, apply definitions stepwise, use logical equivalences, and rewrite as the other side. Make each definitional step explicit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checking relation properties: reflexive, symmetric, transitive
rubrics_metrics.description: To test reflexivity show (x,x) ∈ R for all x in domain; symmetry: show xRy ⇒ yRx; transitivity: show xRy and yRz ⇒ xRz. Provide counterexamples when a property fails.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numerous examples in exercises: inspect pairs, give direct proofs (e.g., x−y integral implies symmetry/transitivity), or produce concrete counterexample pairs for failures. Explain which element or pair violates the property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving an equivalence relation and computing its equivalence classes
rubrics_metrics.description: Show relation is reflexive, symmetric, transitive, then describe classes [a]={x : xRa} often by solving the defining congruence or divisibility condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: congruence-like relations such as 3x−5y even (Problem Section 11.2) and 4|(x+3y). Compute [0],[1],... by substituting representative values and simplifying conditions (e.g., parity, residues mod 4).

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting relations and functions (basic enumeration formulas)
rubrics_metrics.description: Number of relations on A is 2^{|A|^2}; number of functions f:A→B is |B|^{|A|}; number of injective functions when |B|≥|A| is P(|B|,|A|)=|B|(|B|−1)...(|B|−|A|+1); bijections count = |A|! when |A|=|B|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use multiplication principle and consider choices per ordered pair or per domain element. Examples: 2^{36} relations for 6×6, |B|^{|A|} for functions, 7! injective/bijective functions in exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving injectivity by algebraic implication
rubrics_metrics.description: Show f(x)=f(y) implies x=y by algebraic manipulation and elimination; this establishes injectivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: rational function f(x)=(5x+1)/(x−2) injective proof by cross-multiplication leading to 11y=11x ⇒ y=x (Section 12.2). When doing algebraic steps, justify divisions (e.g., denominators nonzero).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving surjectivity by explicit preimage construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Given arbitrary b in codomain, solve f(x)=b for x and show the solution lies in the domain; this demonstrates surjectivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: for f(x)=(5x+1)/(x−2) solve x = (−2b−1)/(5−b), noting b≠5 so denominator nonzero. Always check domain exclusions and existence of solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructing inverses of bijections by solving equations
rubrics_metrics.description: Given bijection f, find f^{-1} by setting y=f(x) and solving for x in terms of y, then state the inverse formula with domain/codomain restrictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: f(n)=2^n inverse log2(n); f(x)=6−x inverse same form; multivariable inverses require solving system for original coordinates (Section 12.5). Explicitly state domain/codomain of inverse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pigeonhole principle applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Partition the universe into k boxes; if more than k objects are chosen then at least one box contains ≥2 objects. Use this to deduce existence statements about remainders or sums/differences divisibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: among 6 integers two have same remainder mod 5; among 7 naturals there is a pair whose sum or difference divisible by 10. Explicitly define partition sets (residue classes) and count.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partition-equivalence correspondence
rubrics_metrics.description: An equivalence relation on A induces a partition of A into equivalence classes; conversely partitions correspond to equivalence relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: partitions induced by congruence modulo 4 produce classes [0],[1],[2],[3]. When asked, list blocks of partition or list equivalence classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function composition computation
rubrics_metrics.description: Compute g∘f and f∘g by substituting the formula for inner function into outer; present resulting explicit formulas for each coordinate (for multivariate functions) or scalar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: given f(x)=x^3 and g(x)=x+1 then g∘f(x)=x^3+1 and f∘g(x)=(x+1)^3; for pairs, substitute coordinate-wise and expand/simplify. Show both compositions separately and simplify.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using counterexamples to disprove blanket claims
rubrics_metrics.description: To disprove a universal claim, provide a specific counterexample (e.g., symmetric+transitive need not imply reflexive).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: relation R = {(a,a),(a,b),(b,a),(b,b)} on {a,b,c} is symmetric and transitive but not reflexive (c lacks self-pair). State clearly why the example violates the purported implication.
